content: The effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives can be diminished when co-administered with certain medications, such as antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and other drugs that enhance the metabolism of contraceptive steroids. This reduction in effectiveness may lead to unintended pregnancies or breakthrough bleeding. Examples of such drugs include rifampin, rifabutin, barbiturates, primidone, phenylbutazone, phenytoin, dexamethasone, carbamazepine, felbamate, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, griseofulvin, and modafinil. In these cases, it is advisable to use an additional non-hormonal method of contraception. There have been reports in the literature of contraceptive failure and breakthrough bleeding associated with the concurrent use of antibiotics such as ampicillin, other penicillins, and tetracyclines. However, clinical pharmacology studies investigating interactions between combined oral contraceptives and these antibiotics have yielded inconsistent results. Certain anti-HIV protease inhibitors have been studied in combination with oral hormonal contraceptives, and significant changes in plasma levels of estrogen and progestin (both increases and decreases) have been observed in some cases. The safety and efficacy of oral contraceptives may be affected when co-administered with anti-HIV protease inhibitors. Healthcare providers should consult the labeling of individual anti-HIV protease inhibitors for detailed drug interaction information. Herbal products containing St. John’s Wort (Hypericum perforatum) may induce hepatic enzymes (cytochrome P450) and p-glycoprotein transporters, potentially reducing the effectiveness of contraceptive steroids. This interaction may also result in breakthrough bleeding. The co-administration of atorvastatin and certain oral contraceptives containing ethinyl estradiol has been shown to increase the area under the curve (AUC) values for ethinyl estradiol by approximately 20%. Ascorbic acid and acetaminophen can increase the bioavailability of ethinyl estradiol by acting as competitive inhibitors of its sulfation in the gastrointestinal wall, a known elimination pathway for ethinyl estradiol. CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as indinavir, itraconazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole, and troleandomycin, may increase plasma hormone levels. Troleandomycin may also elevate the risk of intrahepatic cholestasis when co-administered with combination oral contraceptives. Oral contraceptives may inhibit the metabolism of other compounds, leading to increased plasma concentrations of drugs such as cyclosporin, prednisolone, other corticosteroids, and theophylline. Conversely, decreased plasma concentrations of acetaminophen and increased clearance of temazepam, salicylic acid, morphine, and clofibric acid have been observed due to the induction of conjugation pathways (particularly glucuronidation) when these drugs are administered with oral contraceptives. The prescribing information for concomitant medications should be reviewed to identify potential interactions. Oral contraceptives can also affect laboratory test results. They may increase levels of prothrombin and clotting factors VII, VIII, IX, and X, while decreasing antithrombin III levels. Platelet aggregability induced by norepinephrine may also be increased. Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels may rise, leading to increased circulating total thyroid hormone levels, as measured by protein-bound iodine (PBI), T4 by column, or radioimmunoassay. Free T3 resin uptake may decrease, reflecting elevated TBG levels, but free T4 concentrations remain unchanged. Similarly, corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels may increase, resulting in elevated total circulating corticosteroids and sex steroids, although free or biologically active hormone concentrations remain unaffected. Triglyceride levels may increase, and other lipid and lipoprotein levels may be altered. Glucose tolerance may be reduced. Serum folate levels may be depressed by oral contraceptive therapy, which could be clinically significant if a woman becomes pregnant shortly after discontinuing oral contraceptives. Oral contraceptives are classified as Pregnancy Category X and should not be used during pregnancy due to teratogenic effects. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids and/or their metabolites have been detected in the breast milk of nursing mothers, and a few adverse effects on the child, such as jaundice and breast enlargement, have been reported. Additionally, combination oral contraceptives administered during the postpartum period may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. The safety and efficacy of Aviane tablets have been established in women of reproductive age. These parameters are expected to be similar for postpubertal adolescents under the age of 16 and for users aged 16 years and older. However, the use of Aviane before menarche is not indicated. Aviane has not been studied in women over 65 years of age and is not indicated for this population. Adverse reactions associated with oral contraceptives include an increased risk of thromboembolic and thrombotic disorders (e.g., thrombophlebitis, venous thrombosis with or without pulmonary embolism, mesenteric thrombosis, arterial thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, and cerebral thrombosis), carcinoma of the reproductive organs and breasts, hepatic neoplasia (including hepatic adenomas or benign liver tumors), ocular lesions (e.g., retinal vascular thrombosis), gallbladder disease, carbohydrate and lipid effects, elevated blood pressure, and headaches, including migraines.
